prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its action as an incretin hormone, which made possible a new class of therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the clearest unbroken chain from basic physiology to a therapy that has changed medicine. Holst's human incretin physiology, Drucker's receptor and proglucagon biology, and the identification of the bioactive GLP-1(7-36) peptide together define a mechanism that was then independently validated in large randomized outcome trials for glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The discovery is original, the mechanism is well understood, it has been confirmed by many groups for decades, and the public-health reach is very large. Five of six of us ranked it first, and I do not treat that as merit in itself, but the substantive arguments in the openings converge: it is mature, and further delay brings no scientific benefit. Having read colleagues' attribution arguments, I now move from my opening trio to the physiology-centred set of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov.
statement.case_against: Credit is genuinely contested. Joel Habener, who is not among the credited names, is a serious claimant to the early proglucagon and GLP-1 peptide work, and Mojsov's weight relative to his rests on priority claims that I cannot verify from the supplied material. Leaving out Lotte Bjerre Knudsen means the prize honours physiology and omits the drug development that actually delivered the benefit to patients, which some will see as an incomplete story. A three-person limit makes any version of this prize partial. If the committee judged the credit too tangled, B018 or B043 would be the fallback, but each of those has its own attribution gap.

responses.point: Perlmann proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, treating Knudsen's liraglutide and semaglutide work as an industrial translation contribution and noting that early proglucagon contributors are missing from the credited names.
responses.response: I opened with Knudsen in place of Mojsov and I now think that was the weaker choice. A discovery prize is best anchored on who established the physiology and identified the active peptide, and Knudsen's work builds on that. I still disagree that her contribution is merely industrial: durable acylated agonists are what made the biology usable, and the Nobel record has honoured enabling drug-development steps. But with only three places, the physiology-first trio is the more defensible, and I will go with it. I share your unease about the unresolved Mojsov versus Habener question and cannot settle it from the record.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranks GLP-1 first and also B043 second, arguing that optogenetics is a compound invention in which the choice between Deisseroth, Boyden and Miesenboeck beside the channelrhodopsin discoverers is a real dilemma.
responses.response: I agree that B043 is a compound invention and that three places cannot cover it fairly. My difference is one of rank: I place it fifth, below the CAR-T and antisense candidates, because it is a method whose clinical translation is still early and because the credit dispute is wider than for GLP-1. Optogenetics is a strong tool story, but it is not a stronger case than the incretin chain. I would not let a good methods case displace a mechanism-to-medicine case in the same year.

responses.point: El Manira ranks imatinib (B007) first and GLP-1 fourth, finding imatinib the cleanest proof that inhibiting a driver kinase can control a cancer, and counting it as overdue.
responses.response: I accept that imatinib is a paradigm-setting and fully mature achievement, and that the Druker, Lydon and Sawyers attribution is cleaner than for most candidates. I put it seventh because the discovery-versus-development question is sharpest there: the BCR-ABL fusion and the oncogene work that made the target obvious fall outside the credited names, and the Lasker prize already recognised this trio. GLP-1 has the same tension, which you may fairly point out. I weigh it differently because the incretin physiology is itself the discovery, whereas for imatinib the underlying discovery is credited to others. I would not oppose B007 as a later prize.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks CAR-T second and includes Rosenberg, but acknowledges that Zelig Eshhar, who originated the chimeric receptor concept, is outside the credited names and leaves a real gap in fair allocation.
responses.response: I share the concern about Eshhar, and it is why I omitted Rosenberg in my own CAR-T proposal and kept only June and Sadelain: adoptive cell transfer is a distinct line from receptor engineering, and adding a third name does not repair the missing founder. Including Rosenberg makes the configuration look complete without resolving the attribution problem. I think a CAR-T prize needs a fuller discussion of whether the credited set can be defended at all, so I rank it behind GLP-1 on that ground, not on merit.

uncertainties: Whether Habener's contribution, outside the credited names, outweighs that of Mojsov, and how to cite the identification of the active peptide.
Whether the prize should centre on physiology and peptide identification, or whether a drug-development contribution such as Knudsen's should be included.
Whether the CAR-T and optogenetic attribution problems can be resolved at all with three names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My documented connection is co-authorship of the 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper and shared publications with colleagues, none of which touches the credited names on this shortlist. I have not verified this against every candidate's full publication record.
